context.heading: Brought near
context.body: The word for offering is qorban ("what is brought near"), from the verb qarav, "to come near." An offering was not a fee paid to a distant deity but the way a worshiper drew close to a God who had just moved into the middle of the camp. Mark 7:11 shows the word still in use in Jesus' day.

context.heading: A smell that settles
context.body: The burnt offering is a "pleasing aroma," literally a nichoach ("soothing") smell, from the root for rest. The same root sits in Noah's name and in God's response to Noah's sacrifice (Genesis 8:21). The picture is not a hungry god being fed but divine anger at sin coming to rest.

context.heading: Room for every budget
context.body: The chapter moves from bulls to sheep and goats to birds. A wealthy farmer and a poor family could bring the same offering in different sizes, and both are called a pleasing aroma. Joseph and Mary later brought birds, the offering of the poor (Luke 2:24).

theology.title: A holy God who makes a way
theology.body: Leviticus opens with God calling from the tent, not Moses climbing a mountain. The God who is too holy to approach casually is also the God who designs the approach Himself. Every instruction in this book assumes He wants His people near.

theology.title: The whole thing, given up
theology.body: Nothing of the burnt offering came back to the worshiper. Paul borrows this picture when he urges believers to offer their bodies as living sacrifices (Romans 12:1), and Ephesians 5:2 says Christ gave Himself as a fragrant offering to God. The substitute that Leviticus pictures is fully given in Jesus.

application.title: Hand on the head
application.body: The worshiper did not watch from a distance. He pressed his own hand on the animal and slaughtered it himself, a messy and personal act.
application.question: Where have you kept your faith tidy and distant from the cost of your own sin?

application.title: Generosity is not a size
application.body: God asked the rich for a bull and the poor for a bird, and called both pleasing. Comparison with what others give misses the point.
application.question: What would change if you measured your giving by what it costs you rather than how it looks next to others?

context.heading: A pinch for the fire
context.body: Only a handful of the grain offering was burned. That portion is called the azkarah ("memorial portion"), from the verb "to remember." Scholars debate whether it reminded God of the worshiper or the worshiper of God. Either way, a small part stood for the whole gift, and the rest fed the priests.

context.heading: Salt that does not spoil
context.body: Every grain offering had to be seasoned with salt, called the salt of your God's berit ("covenant"). In the ancient world salt preserved food and was eaten at meals that sealed agreements. Numbers 18:19 calls God's promise to the priests a covenant of salt, meaning lasting and unbreakable.

context.heading: No yeast, no honey
context.body: Yeast and honey both cause fermentation, and Canaanite worship used honey freely. Leaven later became a picture of corruption spreading (1 Corinthians 5:6–8). The rules kept Israel's worship distinct and its symbols clear.

theology.title: God values ordinary work
theology.body: The grain offering came from planting, harvesting, grinding and baking. God received the fruit of everyday labor as worship. Work was never a separate category from devotion in Israel.

theology.title: A God who keeps covenant
theology.body: Salt on every offering reminded Israel that their worship rested on a covenant God would not abandon. Jesus told His followers to be salt (Matthew 5:13), a people preserved by God and preserving others.

application.title: Ordinary offerings
application.body: Flour and oil were kitchen staples, not luxuries. God asked Israel to bring the stuff of daily life.
application.question: Which part of your ordinary week could you hand to God as a deliberate offering?

application.title: The salt test
application.body: Every offering, large or small, carried salt as a reminder of covenant loyalty. Faithfulness was meant to season everything, not only the big moments.
application.question: Where has your commitment to God become flavorless because it shows up only on Sundays?

application.title: Feeding the ones who serve
application.body: Most of the grain went to the priests, who had no farmland. Worship and caring for those who served it were bound together.
application.question: How do you practically support the people who teach and care for you spiritually?

context.heading: All the fat is the LORD's
context.body: The chelev ("fat") around the organs was considered the richest part of the animal, which is why "the fat of the land" means its best produce (Genesis 45:18). Burning it on the altar gave God the choicest portion before the family ate. Verse 17 makes this a permanent rule for all Israel.

context.heading: A meal with God
context.body: Unlike the burnt offering, most of the peace offering was eaten. Ancient covenants were often sealed with a shared meal, and the elders of Israel ate in God's presence at Sinai (Exodus 24:11). The peace offering turned an ordinary family meal into fellowship with the LORD.

context.heading: Male or female
context.body: The burnt offering required a male, but the peace offering could be male or female (v. 1). The rules were less strict because the meal celebrated an existing relationship rather than dealing with sin. Still, the animal had to be without defect.

theology.title: A God who eats with His people
theology.body: The LORD is not only a judge to be appeased but a host who shares a table. Jesus scandalized critics by eating with sinners (Luke 15:2), and the Lord's Supper continues the pattern. Peace with God ends in a meal.

theology.title: Peace already made
theology.body: The peace offering assumes reconciliation has happened. Paul writes that Christ "is our peace" (Ephesians 2:14) and that we have peace with God through Him (Romans 5:1). The celebration rests on what God has already done.

application.title: Best first
application.body: The fat, the best part, went to God before anyone ate. The order said something about priorities.
application.question: What would it look like to give God the first and best portion of your time this week instead of the leftovers?

application.title: Celebrate on purpose
application.body: Israel had a sacrifice designed for joy and thanks. Gratitude was not left to chance; it was built into worship.
application.question: When did you last mark one of God's good gifts with an intentional celebration?

application.title: Invite people in
application.body: A peace offering fed a household, often with neighbors and the poor at the table (Deuteronomy 12:18). Fellowship with God spilled into fellowship with people.
application.question: Who could you invite to your table this month as a way of sharing what God has given you?

context.heading: Sin and its cleanup
context.body: Chatta'ah ("sin") is the same word for the sin and for the offering that deals with it. Many scholars translate it "purification offering," because the blood cleansed the sanctuary that sin had polluted. Sin was not only personal guilt; it left a stain on the place where God lived among His people.

context.heading: Forgiveness promised
context.body: Each section ends with the same line: the priest makes atonement "and he will be salach ("forgiven")." In the Old Testament this verb is used only with God as its subject. People can pardon, but only the LORD forgives in this full sense.

context.heading: Leaders carry more
context.body: A sinning priest "brings guilt on the people" (v. 3), and his blood offering went inside the tent, while an ordinary person's stayed at the outer altar. The higher the role, the deeper the defilement. James 3:1 carries the same principle for teachers.

theology.title: Holy and merciful at once
theology.body: God takes even unintentional sin seriously, yet He provides a remedy for every level of society. Holiness and mercy are not in tension in His character; the sin offering expresses both.

theology.title: Burned outside the camp
theology.body: The remains of the sin offering for the priest and the community were burned outside the camp (vv. 12, 21). Hebrews 13:11–12 sees Jesus suffering outside the city gate to make His people holy through His own blood.

application.title: Unintentional still counts
application.body: Most of our sins are not dramatic rebellion but careless words, ignored needs and blind spots. God still calls them sin and still offers forgiveness.
application.question: Which careless habit have you excused because you never meant to hurt anyone?

application.title: Influence raises the stakes
application.body: A leader's sin cost more because it affected more people. Parents, managers and church leaders carry weight others do not.
application.question: Who is quietly affected by the choices you make in your role at home, work or church?

application.title: When you realize it
application.body: The pattern is: sin, awareness, then action (vv. 14, 23, 28). God did not demand perfection, but He expected a response when the sin became known.
application.question: What have you become aware of recently that you have not yet brought to God?

context.heading: Confession named
context.body: Verse 5 requires the guilty person to yadah ("confess") the specific sin. The same verb usually means to praise or give thanks. In both cases the person openly acknowledges what is true: about God in praise, about oneself in confession.

context.heading: Breaking faith
context.body: Ma'al ("unfaithfully") describes treachery, the kind of betrayal a spouse commits (Numbers 5:12). Here it is misusing what belongs to God, perhaps keeping back a tithe or eating holy food. The guilt offering treats it as a debt that must be repaid with interest.

context.heading: The poor are not shut out
context.body: If a lamb was too expensive, two birds would do; if birds were too much, about two quarts of flour. The sliding scale meant poverty never kept anyone from atonement. God fitted the cost to the person.

theology.title: A God who wants the truth told
theology.body: God could have accepted sacrifices silently, but He requires spoken confession. 1 John 1:9 echoes this: if we confess our sins, He is faithful and just to forgive. Honesty is part of how He heals.

theology.title: The Servant as guilt offering
theology.body: Isaiah 53:10 says the Servant makes His life an asham, a guilt offering. The New Testament applies Isaiah 53 to Jesus (Acts 8:32–35). He paid the debt that sin creates, in full and more.

application.title: Silence can be sin
application.body: Verse 1 names the witness who stays quiet when he knows the truth. Sometimes the wrong is what we fail to say.
application.question: Where are you staying silent when someone needs you to speak the truth?

application.title: Name it specifically
application.body: Verse 5 does not ask for a general admission that everyone sins. It asks the person to confess "the sin he has committed." Vague confession rarely changes anything.
application.question: What specific sin have you been confessing only in general terms?

application.title: Make it right
application.body: Restitution came with an extra fifth. Repentance in Leviticus is not only feeling sorry; it repairs the damage.
application.question: Is there something you owe someone, money, credit or an apology, that you could repay this week?

context.heading: Fraud as unfaithfulness to God
context.body: Verse 2 lists deceiving a neighbor over a deposit, robbery and when a person ashaq ("extorts") a neighbor. This verb describes using power to squeeze the weak, and the prophets use it of oppressing the poor (Amos 4:1). Leviticus calls these crimes unfaithfulness "against the LORD," not merely business disputes.

context.heading: Holy laundry
context.body: The priest wore linen to remove the ashes, then changed clothes before carrying them outside the camp (vv. 10–11). Even the leftovers of worship were handled with care. The most honored servant in Israel spent part of every morning hauling ash.

context.heading: Holiness that spreads
context.body: Verses 18 and 27 say whatever touches the most holy offerings becomes holy, meaning it now belongs to the sanctuary and must be treated that way. Uncleanness was contagious in Israel, but so was holiness. Jesus reverses the usual direction when He touches lepers and they become clean (Mark 1:41).

theology.title: Wronging people wrongs God
theology.body: The guilt offering for fraud went to the LORD, yet restitution went to the neighbor first (v. 5). God refuses to separate worship from how we treat people. Jesus says the same: be reconciled to your brother, then come and offer your gift (Matthew 5:23–24).

theology.title: A way that never closes
theology.body: The fire on the altar burned continually, and a lamb was offered morning and evening. Access to God was not limited to festival days. Hebrews 7:25 says the risen Christ always lives to intercede for those who come to God through Him.

application.title: Repay before you pray
application.body: The cheater had to return what he took, plus a fifth, on the day he brought his offering. Worship did not cover what restitution could fix.
application.question: Is there a debt or broken promise you have tried to pray away instead of making right?

application.title: Tend the fire
application.body: Someone had to add wood every morning, or the fire went out. Spiritual life is often kept alive by unglamorous daily habits.
application.question: What small, daily practice keeps your faith burning, and which one has quietly lapsed?

application.title: Ash duty
application.body: The priest who stood before God also carried the ashes out. No task in God's service was beneath him.
application.question: Which humble task at home, work or church have you been avoiding because it feels beneath you?

context.heading: Three reasons to celebrate
context.body: A peace offering could be for thanksgiving, for a vow, or as a nedavah ("freewill offering"), a gift given simply because the worshiper wanted to. Thanksgiving answered something God had done, a vow kept a promise made in need, and the freewill gift came from overflowing gratitude. The rules for eating differed slightly for each.

context.heading: Cut off
context.body: Eating holy meat while unclean meant being karat ("cut off") from one's people. Scholars debate whether this meant exile, early death at God's hand, or the end of one's family line. Whatever its form, it signaled that treating holy things carelessly was serious.

context.heading: The priests' share
context.body: The breast and right thigh of the peace offering went to the priests (vv. 31–34). The breast was waved before the LORD, a gesture showing it was given to God first and then handed back to His servants. This was the priests' wages, since they had no land.

theology.title: God welcomes gratitude
theology.body: Of all the sacrifices, God gave the most detail for the one expressing thanks. He is not a God who only tolerates worship but one who delights in a grateful people. Hebrews 13:15 calls praise a sacrifice believers still offer.

theology.title: Holy things are not casual
theology.body: Uncleanness and holiness could not sit at the same table. Paul warns the Corinthians against eating the Lord's Supper in an unworthy manner (1 Corinthians 11:27–29). God's gifts are generous, but they are still holy.

application.title: Eat it today
application.body: Thanksgiving meat had to be eaten the same day (v. 15), which usually meant inviting others to share it. Gratitude was meant to be immediate and communal.
application.question: Who could share in your thanks for something God has done this week?

application.title: Keep the vow
application.body: Vow offerings existed because people made promises to God in hard times. Leviticus expects those promises to be kept when the crisis passes.
application.question: What did you promise God in a difficult season that you have not followed through on?

application.title: Generosity with no reason
application.body: The freewill offering was given because the worshiper wanted to, not because anything required it. It is the purest form of giving.
application.question: When did you last give something away with no obligation, occasion or expectation behind it?

context.heading: Filling the hands
context.body: "It will take seven days to ordain you" is literally "to male ("fill") your hands." The phrase may picture the priest's hands filled with the offerings he would present (vv. 26–28). Ordination was not a title conferred but hands loaded with work for God.

context.heading: Set apart, not superior
context.body: Moses qadash ("consecrated") Aaron and his garments by sprinkling them with oil and blood. The verb means to make holy, to set apart for God's exclusive use. The priests were not more valuable people; they were people assigned to a sacred purpose.

context.heading: Exactly as commanded
context.body: Some form of "as the LORD commanded Moses" appears again and again in this chapter (vv. 4, 9, 13, 17, 21, 29, 36). After the golden calf (Exodus 32), Israel is learning to worship God His way. The repetition is the point: careful obedience.

theology.title: Priests who need atonement
theology.body: Aaron needed a sin offering before he could offer for anyone else (v. 14). Hebrews 7:26–27 contrasts this with Jesus, who had no sin of His own and offered Himself once for all. The best human priest still needed a Savior.

theology.title: A priesthood for all God's people
theology.body: Only Aaron's family served at the altar, but God's goal was always wider: Israel was to be "a kingdom of priests" (Exodus 19:6). Peter applies this to the church as a royal priesthood (1 Peter 2:9). Every believer now has access through Christ.

application.title: Ear, hand, foot
application.body: Blood on the ear, thumb and toe dedicated what the priests heard, did and where they went. Holiness reached their whole bodies, not just the time spent in the tent.
application.question: Which of the three, what you listen to, what you do, or where you go, most needs to be handed back to God?

application.title: Seven days of waiting
application.body: The priests sat at the entrance for a full week before serving. Preparation was part of the calling, not a delay to it.
application.question: Where are you impatient to serve when God may be using a season of waiting to prepare you?

context.heading: He will appear
context.body: Moses tells the people that today the LORD will ra'ah ("appear") to them (v. 4). The verb means "to be seen." Everything in chapters 1 to 8 had been leading here: sacrifices and priests were never ends in themselves but the way to God's visible presence among His people.

context.heading: Hands raised in blessing
context.body: Aaron lifted his hands and barakh ("blessed") the people (v. 22). Many think he used words like the priestly blessing later recorded in Numbers 6:24–26. In Hebrew thought, a blessing spoken by God's appointed servant actually conveyed God's favor.

context.heading: Joy and the ground
context.body: When fire fell, the people shouted for joy and fell facedown (v. 24). The two responses belong together. Worship in Israel was both loud celebration and humbled awe.

theology.title: God keeps His word
theology.body: Moses said the LORD would appear, and He did. The God of Leviticus is not unpredictable; He binds Himself to promises and fulfills them. The fire that consumed the offering was His public acceptance of the worship He had designed.

theology.title: The final blessing
theology.body: Luke ends his Gospel with Jesus lifting His hands to bless His disciples before He was taken up (Luke 24:50–51). The great High Priest completes the work Aaron pictured and blesses His people from God's presence.

application.title: Preparation before presence
application.body: Aaron offered for himself before he offered for the people. Leaders who skip their own repentance have little to give others.
application.question: What do you need to settle with God before you try to help someone else with theirs?

application.title: Shouting and bowing
application.body: Israel's worship held loud joy and face-down reverence in the same moment. Most of us lean naturally toward one.
application.question: Which do you tend to leave out, celebration or awe, and what would it take to recover it?

application.title: Leave with a blessing
application.body: The service ended not with a list of duties but with a blessing. God's people walked out carrying His favor.
application.question: How would your week change if you believed God's blessing went with you out of Sunday worship?

context.heading: Aaron's silence
context.body: After his sons died, "Aaron damam ("remained silent")." The verb can mean to be still or stunned. It is not necessarily calm acceptance; it may be grief too deep for words. The same root appears in Psalm 4:4 and Psalm 62:1, where silence before God is a form of trust.

context.heading: Know the difference
context.body: The priests' job was to badal ("distinguish") between holy and common, clean and unclean (v. 10). The same verb describes God separating light from darkness in Genesis 1:4. Priests carried that ordering work into daily life and taught it to Israel.

context.heading: A hard scene with care
context.body: This is one of the most painful moments in Scripture: a father losing two sons on the day of his greatest joy. Readers who have suffered sudden loss may find it hard to read. The text does not ask us to feel nothing; it shows Aaron grieving and God dealing gently with him at the end of the chapter (vv. 16–20).

theology.title: Holiness is not a toy
theology.body: "To those who come near Me I will show My holiness" (v. 3). Being close to God brings greater responsibility, not license. Acts 5 records a similar moment at the start of the church, and Hebrews 12:28–29 reminds believers that our God is a consuming fire.

theology.title: Mercy within holiness
theology.body: When Aaron's surviving sons did not eat the sin offering, Moses was angry, but he accepted Aaron's explanation (vv. 19–20). The same God who judged careless worship also understood a grieving father. His holiness is never cold.

application.title: Sincere is not enough
application.body: Nadab and Abihu were enthusiastic, but they worshiped on their own terms. Good intentions do not replace obedience.
application.question: Where are you serving God in a way that suits you rather than in the way He has asked?

application.title: Clear heads
application.body: Verse 9 bans alcohol for priests on duty so they could judge clearly. Anything that dulls judgment can damage our ability to serve others well.
application.question: What habit, substance or screen dulls your judgment when people need you most?

application.title: Room for grief
application.body: Aaron could not eat that day, and Moses let it stand. Faithfulness and grief can live in the same person.
application.question: Who in your life needs permission to grieve without being rushed back to normal?

context.heading: Be holy because I am
context.body: The chapter's punchline is not hygiene but identity: "be qadosh ("holy"), because I am holy" (vv. 44–45). Holiness means being set apart for God and sharing His character. Peter quotes this line to Gentile Christians who never kept these food laws (1 Peter 1:15–16), applying its heart to all of life.

context.heading: Detestable, not evil
context.body: Animals like shellfish are sheqets ("detestable") to Israel (v. 10). The word means something to be treated as off limits, not a creature God hates; Genesis 1:31 calls everything He made very good. The ban was about Israel's table, not the animal's worth.

context.heading: Categories and order
context.body: Clean land animals both chew the cud and have split hooves; clean fish have fins and scales. Many scholars think creatures that did not fit their category neatly were treated as unclean, mirroring the order of creation in Genesis 1. Others stress health or separation from pagan rites. The text itself gives only holiness as the reason.

theology.title: Redemption comes before rules
theology.body: Verse 45 grounds the food laws in the exodus: "I am the LORD, who brought you up out of the land of Egypt." God did not give rules so Israel could earn rescue. He rescued them first, then showed them how to live as His people.

theology.title: Fulfilled, not discarded
theology.body: Jesus declared all foods clean (Mark 7:19), and Peter's vision in Acts 10 taught that Gentiles were no longer to be treated as unclean. The food laws had marked Israel off from the nations. In Christ, God forms one people from both, and holiness moves from the menu to the heart.

application.title: Holy in the kitchen
application.body: Israel met God's holiness three times a day at meals. Faithfulness was practiced in the most ordinary choices.
application.question: Which everyday routine, eating, scrolling or spending, could become a deliberate place to honor God?

application.title: Freedom without contempt
application.body: Paul tells Christians not to despise others over food and holy days (Romans 14:3). Freedom in Christ can turn into pride if we are not careful.
application.question: Whose convictions about food, drink or entertainment do you quietly look down on?

application.title: Distinct, not odd
application.body: Israel's diet made them noticeably different from their neighbors. Holiness will sometimes make you stand out.
application.question: Where is God asking you to be visibly different from the people around you, even if it costs you?

context.heading: Clean again
context.body: The goal of the chapter is the final word: she will taher ("be clean") (v. 8). The verb describes restoration to full participation in worship. Her recovery time ended not with suspicion but with the priest declaring her clean and welcome at the sanctuary.

context.heading: Forty and eighty days
context.body: After a boy the mother waited a total of forty days; after a girl, eighty. No one knows the reason for sure. Some point to ancient beliefs about recovery, others to the girl's own future as a mother. The offering at the end was identical for both, so the difference is not about the child's worth.

context.heading: Recovery built in
context.body: The weeks of purification also protected new mothers. She did not have to go to the sanctuary or handle holy food while her body healed and she cared for a newborn. The law gave her space that a busy farming household might not have given otherwise.

theology.title: Jesus under the law
theology.body: Mary brought two birds, the offering of the poor (Luke 2:22–24). The Son of God was born into a poor family that kept this law faithfully. Galatians 4:4–5 says He was "born under the law, to redeem those under the law."

theology.title: God in the ordinary seasons
theology.body: A whole chapter of Scripture is given to a new mother. God's law reached into the most private and physical seasons of life. He is not interested only in temple days but in the delivery room and the weeks that follow.

application.title: Care for new mothers
application.body: Israel's law carved out time for a mother to recover. Many new parents today are rushed back to work and routine with little support.
application.question: What practical help could you offer a new parent you know this month?

application.title: No one priced out
application.body: The poor mother brought two birds instead of a lamb, and she was just as clean. God made sure finances never barred anyone from His presence.
application.question: Where might cost be quietly keeping people out of your church or community, and what could you do about it?

application.title: Mark the milestone
application.body: The new mother's journey ended at the sanctuary with an offering. A birth was brought before God, not just celebrated at home.
application.question: How do you bring the big milestones of your family's life before God, not just before friends and followers?

context.heading: A touch or a mark
context.body: The word for the condition is nega ("plague"), literally a "touch" or "stroke." It can describe any mark, sore or affliction. English versions vary between "infection," "sore" and "disease" in the same chapter because the Hebrew word covers them all.

context.heading: Living outside the camp
context.body: An infected person had to yashav ("dwell") alone outside the camp (v. 46). Torn clothes, loose hair and a covered upper lip were signs of mourning (v. 45). The person grieved their own separation from community and worship, and warned others away by calling, "Unclean, unclean!"

context.heading: Careful, not hasty
context.body: The priest examined, isolated the person for seven days, and examined again before deciding (vv. 4–6). Many cases turned out to be harmless. The law guarded both the community from contamination and the individual from a rushed verdict.

theology.title: Holiness and wholeness
theology.body: The camp was where God lived, so anything that pictured decay and death had to stay outside it. Skin conditions that made a person look like they were wasting away were a vivid picture of how sin corrupts. God's presence is a place of life.

theology.title: The touch that cleanses
theology.body: When a man with this disease begged Jesus, He reached out and touched him (Mark 1:40–42). Under the law, touching made the healthy unclean. With Jesus, His touch made the unclean whole. He then sent the man to the priest, honoring Leviticus 14.

application.title: Slow to declare
application.body: The priest waited a week before making a call. Quick judgments about people often turn out to be wrong.
application.question: Whom have you labeled too quickly, and what would it look like to take a second look?

application.title: The loneliness of sickness
application.body: The infected person lived apart, sometimes for years. Long illness still isolates people today, even in a crowded church.
application.question: Who do you know whose illness has slowly cut them off, and how could you close that distance?

application.title: Clothes and walls
application.body: The same rules covered mold in garments (vv. 47–59). God cared about the condition of ordinary household things.
application.question: What is slowly spreading in your home, a habit, a tension, a mess, that needs to be dealt with before it ruins more?

context.heading: Living water
context.body: The first bird was killed over chay ("living") water, meaning fresh running water from a spring or stream (v. 5). Jesus uses the same image when He offers "living water" (John 4:10; 7:38). Stagnant water could not picture new life; running water could.

context.heading: Set free
context.body: The priest dipped the live bird in the blood of the first and would shalach ("release") it into the open field (v. 7). One bird died, one flew away free. The picture of death and release mirrors the two goats of the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16).

context.heading: Treated like a priest
context.body: Blood and oil were put on the healed person's right ear, thumb and big toe (v. 14), exactly as at the ordination of priests (Leviticus 8:23–24). The person who had been furthest outside the camp was restored with the same honor as those who served nearest to God.

theology.title: The God who restores
theology.body: The priest went outside the camp to the sick person (v. 3), not the other way round. God's law moved toward the outsider. Hebrews 13:12–13 says Jesus suffered outside the gate and calls believers to go to Him there.

theology.title: Jesus sends them back
theology.body: Jesus told healed lepers to show themselves to the priests and offer what Moses commanded (Mark 1:44; Luke 17:14). He was not dismissing Leviticus but fulfilling it. Only one of the ten in Luke returned to give thanks, and he was a Samaritan.

application.title: Go outside the camp
application.body: The priest left the center to meet the excluded. Restoration started with someone willing to go to them.
application.question: Who is on the edge of your church or family that you could go to this week?

application.title: Welcome all the way back
application.body: A recovered person was not merely tolerated; they were anointed like a priest. Restoration in God's people should be generous, not grudging.
application.question: When someone returns after failure or illness, do you welcome them fully or keep them at arm's length?

application.title: Inspect the house
application.body: Mold in a house was not painted over; the stones were scraped and replaced, and if it kept spreading the house came down (vv. 39–45). Some problems need removal, not cover.
application.question: What in your home or habits are you covering up when it really needs to be removed?

context.heading: Kept separate
context.body: Verse 31 explains the whole chapter: Israel was to be nazar ("kept separate") from uncleanness so they would not defile God's dwelling. The verb is related to Nazirite, a person set apart. The point was not that bodies are shameful but that God's presence required careful boundaries.

context.heading: God's tent among them
context.body: The danger in verse 31 is defiling God's mishkan ("tabernacle"), literally His "dwelling place," which was "among them." The more seriously Israel took God's nearness, the more seriously they took ordinary impurity. Distance would have made these rules unnecessary.

context.heading: Normal and not shameful
context.body: Marital intimacy made a couple unclean only until evening after washing (v. 18). Sex itself was not sinful; God blessed it in Genesis 1:28. Many scholars think this rule kept Israel's worship distinct from Canaanite fertility cults, where sex was part of religious ritual.

theology.title: Life and holiness
theology.body: Many scholars note that these discharges involve the loss of life giving fluids. The LORD is the living God, and the laws kept anything associated with loss of life away from His dwelling. He is the source of life, not death.

theology.title: Power that flows out
theology.body: The woman in Mark 5:25–34 had a flow of blood for twelve years and touched Jesus in a crowd. By law, her touch should have made Him unclean. Instead, power went out from Him and healed her, and He called her "Daughter."

application.title: Bodies are not shameful
application.body: Scripture speaks about bodily functions plainly and without embarrassment. Shame about the body is often something we absorb from others, not from God.
application.question: What unhelpful shame about your body have you carried that Scripture does not place on you?

application.title: Respecting limits
application.body: Some uncleanness was simply part of being human, but it still meant waiting and washing. Honoring God sometimes means respecting limits we did not choose.
application.question: What limit in your health or season of life are you resisting instead of honoring?

application.title: Make it safe to speak
application.body: The woman in Mark 5 suffered quietly for twelve years and approached Jesus from behind. Private health struggles often stay hidden out of embarrassment.
application.question: How could you make it easier for someone around you to talk about a health struggle they keep private?

context.heading: The place of covering
context.body: The lid on the ark was the kapporet ("mercy seat"), from the same root as kaphar, "to atone." It was the place where atonement blood was sprinkled and where God said He would appear (v. 2). The Greek Old Testament translated it hilasterion, the word Paul uses of Christ in Romans 3:25 and Hebrews uses in 9:5.

context.heading: Plain linen
context.body: On this one day the high priest set aside his gold and colored garments and wore plain linen (v. 4). He entered God's presence dressed more like a servant than a dignitary. The most important act of the year was done in humility.

context.heading: Complete rest
context.body: The day was a shabbaton ("Sabbath of complete rest") (v. 31), with no work of any kind and a call to humble oneself, which Jews have long understood as fasting. Israel contributed nothing to the atonement. They stopped, humbled themselves and let God's appointed sacrifice do its work.

theology.title: Once a year, then once for all
theology.body: Aaron could not enter "freely" (v. 2); he went in once a year, with blood, after offering for his own sin. Hebrews 9:7–12 contrasts this with Christ, who entered the true sanctuary once for all with His own blood and secured an eternal redemption. Leviticus 16 is the background for much of Hebrews 9 and 10.

theology.title: The curtain opened
theology.body: The whole ceremony assumed a curtain separating the people from God's presence. When Jesus died, the temple curtain was torn from top to bottom (Matthew 27:51). Hebrews 10:19–22 invites believers to enter with confidence by the new and living way He opened.

application.title: Stop and humble yourself
application.body: The holiest day of Israel's year was a day of no work and self denial. Atonement was received, not achieved.
application.question: When did you last set aside a whole day, or even an hour, simply to stop and receive God's forgiveness?

application.title: Don't fetch the goat
application.body: The goat carried the people's sins into the wilderness and did not come back. Many believers keep going out to retrieve guilt God has already removed.
application.question: Which forgiven sin do you keep dragging back into your present?

application.title: Confidence, not casualness
application.body: Aaron entered trembling, once a year. Believers can now approach God boldly through Christ (Hebrews 4:16), but boldness is not the same as treating Him lightly.
application.question: Do you tend to approach God with too much fear or too little reverence, and what would balance look like?

context.heading: Sacrifices in the open
context.body: Some Israelites had been offering zevach ("sacrifices") out in the fields (v. 5), away from the tabernacle and the priests. Every slaughter of a sacrificial animal was now to happen at the Tent of Meeting. Worship was to be centered on God's chosen place, not scattered across private altars.

context.heading: Spiritual adultery
context.body: Verse 7 says the people had zanah ("prostituted themselves") with goat demons, probably wilderness spirits that people in the region feared and appeased. The prophets regularly picture idolatry as unfaithfulness in marriage (Hosea 2; Ezekiel 16). Israel's relationship with God was a covenant of love, and idols broke it.

context.heading: Cover it with dirt
context.body: Even a hunter had to drain a wild animal's blood and cover it with dirt (v. 13). The life of every creature belonged to God, and its blood was treated with respect, almost like a burial. God's concern reached beyond the altar to the hunting field.

theology.title: Atonement is God's gift
theology.body: "I have given it to you to make atonement" (v. 11). Sacrifice was not humanity's idea for bribing God; God Himself provided the means. The cross follows the same pattern: God gave His Son (John 3:16; Romans 3:25).

theology.title: Blood in the New Testament
theology.body: Hebrews 9:22 echoes this chapter's logic, and Jesus says His blood is "the blood of the covenant, poured out for many" (Mark 14:24). The Jerusalem council asked Gentile believers to avoid eating blood (Acts 15:20), likely to keep fellowship with Jewish Christians. Christians today differ on whether that request still binds.

application.title: No private altars
application.body: Offering in the open fields let people mix true worship with hedging their bets on other spirits. Private, unaccountable religion drifts easily.
application.question: Where has your faith become a private arrangement with no one to ask hard questions?

application.title: The things we appease
application.body: Israel feared wilderness spirits and offered to them just in case. Modern people appease other powers: approval, money, luck.
application.question: What do you quietly offer things to just in case God is not enough?

application.title: Life is not cheap
application.body: Even a hunted bird's blood was drained and covered with care. Life, any life, belonged to God and was not to be treated carelessly.
application.question: Where has familiarity with violence, in news, games or entertainment, made life seem cheap to you?

context.heading: Exposing nakedness
context.body: "Expose the ervah ("nakedness")" is a Hebrew way of describing sexual relations. Ancient households were large, with several generations and wives living together. These laws protected women and children inside the family from those who had power over them.

context.heading: The word abomination
context.body: Verse 22 forbids a man lying with a male as with a woman and calls it to'evah ("abomination"), something detestable to God. The same word describes pride (Proverbs 16:5), dishonest business (Deuteronomy 25:16) and child sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31). It marks a strong moral judgment across many areas of life, not only sexual ones.

context.heading: A land that vomits
context.body: The land is pictured as a body that cannot keep down what poisons it and will qo ("vomit") out its inhabitants (vv. 25, 28). The warning applied to Israel as much as to the Canaanites. Israel's later exile was understood as this warning coming true.

theology.title: God's standard for everyone
theology.body: God judged the Canaanites for these practices and warned Israel that it would face the same judgment (v. 28). He shows no favoritism. His holiness is not tribal; it is the standard for the whole earth.

theology.title: Law, life and the gospel
theology.body: "The man who does these things will live by them" (v. 5) is quoted by Paul to show that no one keeps the law perfectly (Romans 10:5; Galatians 3:12). Christians apply Old Testament law in different ways; many distinguish moral, civil and ceremonial laws. The New Testament restates a sexual ethic (1 Corinthians 6:9–11) and then adds, "such were some of you. But you were washed."

application.title: Boundaries protect
application.body: These laws drew clear lines in places where the powerful could easily exploit the vulnerable. God's boundaries are often protection, not restriction.
application.question: Which boundary in your life or family exists to protect someone more vulnerable than you?

application.title: Customs around you
application.body: Israel had to unlearn Egypt and resist Canaan at the same time. Every culture normalizes something God does not.
application.question: Which assumption about sex, money or success have you absorbed from your culture without checking it against Scripture?

application.title: Holiness with humility
application.body: The same chapter that names sins also warns Israel it could fall into them. Moral clarity without humility turns into self righteousness.
application.question: How can you hold God's standards firmly while speaking about them with the humility of someone who also needs grace?

context.heading: Who is my neighbor?
context.body: "Love your re'a ("neighbor") as yourself" (v. 18) appears in a list of laws against grudges, revenge and slander. In context re'a means a fellow Israelite, but verse 34 stretches the same love to the foreigner: "love him as yourself." A lawyer later asked Jesus where the line was, and He answered with the Good Samaritan (Luke 10:29–37).

context.heading: Wages by nightfall
context.body: Day laborers lived hand to mouth, so withholding wages "until morning" (v. 13) could mean a family went hungry. Deuteronomy 24:14–15 repeats the rule and James 5:4 condemns employers who cheat workers. Justice in Leviticus is concrete and immediate.

context.heading: I am the LORD
context.body: The phrase "I am the LORD" punctuates this chapter fifteen times. Each law ends by pointing back to God's character. Israel was not following abstract ethics but reflecting the One who had rescued them.

theology.title: Ethics flow from God's character
theology.body: "Be holy because I, the LORD your God, am holy" (v. 2) opens a chapter about honest scales, fair courts, elderly people and immigrants. God's holiness is not distant; it shows up in how we treat the vulnerable.

theology.title: The royal law
theology.body: Jesus called verse 18 the second greatest commandment (Matthew 22:39). Paul says it sums up the law (Romans 13:9) and James calls it "the royal law" (James 2:8). Love fulfills what the law was always aiming at.

application.title: Say it to their face
application.body: Verse 17 forbids hating in your heart and requires frank rebuke instead. Silent resentment is treated as a sin, not a virtue.
application.question: Is there someone you are quietly resenting whom you need to speak to honestly and kindly?

application.title: Pay on time
application.body: Holding back what you owe to workers was a matter of holiness. Late invoices, unpaid favors and delayed repayments hurt real people.
application.question: Who are you making wait for money, credit or thanks that you owe them now?

application.title: Stand up for the gray head
application.body: Verse 32 tells Israel to rise in the presence of the elderly. Respect for older people was part of fearing God.
application.question: How could you show honor to an older person in your church or family this week?

context.heading: The God who sanctifies
context.body: "I am the LORD who qadash ("sanctifies") you" (v. 8). Verse 7 tells Israel to consecrate themselves, and verse 8 says God is the one who does it. Holiness is both a command to obey and a gift God gives.

context.heading: Set apart from the nations
context.body: God says He has badal ("set apart") Israel from the peoples (v. 24), the same verb used for separating clean from unclean animals in verse 25. Israel's careful distinctions in food and daily life mirrored God's choice of them as His own.

context.heading: Severe penalties
context.body: Many crimes here, including the same sexual act forbidden in 18:22 (v. 13), carry the death penalty in Israel's civil law. Christians apply these laws in different ways. The New Testament church did not carry out civil penalties; Paul instead calls for church discipline aimed at repentance (1 Corinthians 5:12–13; 2 Corinthians 2:6–8).

theology.title: God defends the defenseless
theology.body: Child sacrifice to Molech heads the list, and God says He will set His face against anyone who does it and anyone who looks the other way (vv. 2–5). The God of Leviticus fiercely defends children, the most vulnerable members of any society.

theology.title: Holy to Me
theology.body: "You are to be holy to Me because I, the LORD, am holy, and I have set you apart from the nations to be My own" (v. 26). God's laws were not arbitrary hurdles but the shape of belonging to Him. Peter applies this identity to the church (1 Peter 2:9).

application.title: Seeking other voices
application.body: Verse 6 treats consulting mediums as unfaithfulness. Horoscopes, fortune telling and endless online advice can quietly replace seeking God.
application.question: Where do you turn first for guidance when you are anxious about the future?

application.title: Don't look away
application.body: God condemned not only those who sacrificed children but the community that closed its eyes (v. 4). Silence can make us complicit.
application.question: What harm to a vulnerable person have you noticed and chosen not to see?

application.title: Words about parents
application.body: Verse 9 treats cursing father or mother as a grave offense. How we speak about our parents shapes the people listening, especially our children.
application.question: What do the people around you learn about honoring parents from the way you talk about yours?

context.heading: The food of God
context.body: Offerings are called "the lechem ("food") of their God" (v. 6). This is picture language for a shared meal, not a claim that God needs feeding. Psalm 50:12–13 makes the point directly: if God were hungry, He would not tell us. The image stresses fellowship at His table.

context.heading: A priest close to life
context.body: The high priest could not go near a dead body, even for his father or mother (v. 11). The sanctuary was the place of the living God, and the one who served there most closely had to embody that. Ordinary priests could mourn close relatives (vv. 2–3).

context.heading: Excluded from serving, not from provision
context.body: A priest with a defect could not offer sacrifices but could still "eat the most holy food of his God" (v. 22). He remained a priest, supported and fed from the altar. The restriction was about the symbolism of wholeness in the act of offering, not about his standing before God.

theology.title: A priest without blemish
theology.body: Every priestly requirement pointed to a standard no human priest could fully meet. Hebrews 7:26 describes Jesus as holy, innocent, unstained and separated from sinners. He is the unblemished High Priest these rules pictured.

theology.title: The banquet opened wide
theology.body: Jesus told His followers to invite "the poor, the crippled, the lame and the blind" to their feasts (Luke 14:13), and in His parable those very people fill the master's house (Luke 14:21). In Christ, the symbolic boundaries of the tabernacle give way to a table where all who come by faith are welcome.

application.title: Leaders and their homes
application.body: The priest's family life was part of his service (vv. 7–9). Those who lead in public are shaped by what happens at home.
application.question: What is your home life saying about the faith you profess in public?

application.title: Worth is not ability
application.body: The priest with a disability was still fed from the most holy food. A role he could not fill did not cancel his place.
application.question: Whom do you value mainly for what they can do, and how could you honor them for who they are?

context.heading: Accepted on your behalf
context.body: An offering with a defect "will not be ratson ("accepted") on your behalf" (v. 20). The word means favor or goodwill. The sacrifice stood in for the worshiper, so a damaged substitute was no substitute at all.

context.heading: Acknowledged as holy
context.body: "I must be qadash ("acknowledged as holy") among the Israelites. I am the LORD who sanctifies you" (v. 32). The same verb appears in both halves: Israel was to treat God as holy, and God was the one making Israel holy. The relationship ran both ways.

context.heading: Seven days with mother
context.body: A newborn animal had to stay with its mother for seven days, and a mother and its young could not be slaughtered on the same day (vv. 27–28). Even in the sacrificial system, God built in a small mercy. Deuteronomy 22:6–7 shows similar care for a mother bird.

theology.title: God deserves the best
theology.body: Centuries later, Malachi rebuked priests who offered blind and lame animals and asked whether their governor would accept such a gift (Malachi 1:8). The God who gave Israel the best land expected the best in return. Leftovers communicated contempt.

theology.title: The spotless Lamb
theology.body: Peter says believers were redeemed "with the precious blood of Christ, a lamb without blemish or spot" (1 Peter 1:19). The sacrifices of Leviticus 22 had to be flawless because they pointed toward the only perfect sacrifice.

application.title: No damaged goods
application.body: Bringing a flawed animal let a worshiper look generous while losing nothing of value. It is easy to give God what we would have thrown away.
application.question: Where are you giving God your leftovers, time, money or energy, while keeping the best for yourself?

application.title: Small mercies matter
application.body: God cared whether a calf stayed with its mother for a week. Faithfulness shows up in small kindnesses no one would notice.
application.question: What small act of compassion could you build into a routine that currently has none?

application.title: Holiness at the family table
application.body: Only the priest's household could eat the holy food, and who belonged there was carefully defined. Belonging brought privileges and responsibilities.
application.question: How do you treat the privileges of belonging to God's family: as rights you are owed or gifts you are entrusted with?

context.heading: The first sheaf
context.body: At harvest Israel brought a sheaf of the reshit ("firstfruits") to the priest before eating any of the new crop (vv. 10, 14). The first portion was a pledge that the whole harvest belonged to God. Paul calls the risen Christ "the firstfruits of those who have fallen asleep" (1 Corinthians 15:20): His resurrection guarantees ours.

context.heading: A week in shelters
context.body: For the Feast of Booths Israel lived in a sukkah ("booth"), a temporary shelter of branches, for seven days (v. 42). It reminded them how God had sheltered them in the wilderness (v. 43). John 1:14 says the Word "made His dwelling" among us, using a verb related to the Greek word for tent.

context.heading: The poor in the middle
context.body: Right in the middle of the feast list, verse 22 repeats the command to leave the edges of the field for the poor and the foreigner. Israel's celebrations were never to forget those without a harvest of their own.

theology.title: God orders time
theology.body: Israel's calendar circled around God's acts: creation rest, rescue from Egypt and provision in the wilderness. Paul calls Christ our Passover lamb (1 Corinthians 5:7), and the Spirit came at the Feast of Weeks (Acts 2:1). Colossians 2:16–17 calls the feasts shadows of the reality found in Christ.

theology.title: A God who loves a celebration
theology.body: These were not grim religious duties. Booths was explicitly a time to rejoice (v. 40). The LORD built joy, feasting and rest into the life of His people by command.

application.title: Your calendar preaches
application.body: Israel's year was shaped around remembering God. Our calendars also reveal what we treat as most important.
application.question: If someone studied your calendar for a month, what would they conclude you worship?

application.title: Remember the tent
application.body: Living in a booth for a week reminded comfortable farmers that they had once been homeless wanderers. Prosperity tends to make us forget.
application.question: What practice could remind you of where God brought you from?

application.title: Firstfruits, not last
application.body: Israel gave the first sheaf before tasting the harvest. Giving first is an act of trust; giving last is an act of convenience.
application.question: What would change if God received the first portion of your paycheck, schedule or energy instead of the last?

context.heading: A limit on revenge
context.body: "Eye tachat ("for") eye" (v. 20) means "in place of": the penalty must match the injury and go no further. In a world of blood feuds, it capped revenge and kept punishment in the courts. When Jesus says "turn the other cheek" (Matthew 5:38–39), He addresses personal retaliation, not the justice system.

context.heading: The lamp before God
context.body: Aaron tended the lamps on the gold menorah ("lampstand") from evening to morning (vv. 3–4). Its light burned in the Holy Place, where no window let in the sun. It pictured God's presence giving light among His people.

context.heading: One law for all
context.body: The man who blasphemed had an Egyptian father, yet the same law applied to him as to any Israelite (v. 22). Injury laws likewise protected native and foreigner equally. Justice in Israel was not to depend on a person's background.

theology.title: God's name is holy
theology.body: The third commandment forbade misusing God's name (Exodus 20:7). Here it is taken with life and death seriousness. Ironically, Jesus was later condemned for blasphemy (Mark 14:64) because He spoke the truth about who He was.

theology.title: Justice that is measured
theology.body: God's law demanded neither too little nor too much. Proportion is part of His justice. The cross shows both: sin's penalty fully paid, and mercy freely offered.

application.title: Casual with His name
application.body: The blasphemer cursed God in the heat of a fight. Many people use God's name as a casual exclamation without thinking.
application.question: How do you speak about God when you are angry, careless or joking?

application.title: Even the score, then stop
application.body: Eye for eye forbade escalation. In conflicts, we usually want to hit back harder than we were hit.
application.question: In a current conflict, what would it look like to refuse to escalate even when you could?

application.title: How it started
application.body: The blasphemy began as an ordinary fight in the camp (v. 10). Anger has a way of carrying our words further than we ever meant them to go.
application.question: What do your words in anger reveal about what you really think of God and of people?

context.heading: The family redeemer
context.body: If an Israelite fell into poverty and sold land, his ga'al ("kinsman redeemer") could buy it back (v. 25). Boaz plays this role for Ruth and Naomi (Ruth 4:4–10). Isaiah repeatedly calls the LORD Israel's Redeemer (Isaiah 43:14; 44:6).

context.heading: Tenants of God
context.body: "The land is Mine, and you are but foreigners and toshav ("residents") with Me" (v. 23). Israelites owned their land only as tenants of God. That is why it could be leased until Jubilee but never sold permanently.

context.heading: No profit from the poor
context.body: Israelites were not to charge interest to a poor countryman or sell him food for profit (vv. 36–37). The law did not ban business, but it refused to let one family's hardship become another's income.

theology.title: The year of the LORD's favor
theology.body: Jesus opened His ministry by reading Isaiah 61:1–2, which draws on Jubilee language of release, and said, "Today this Scripture is fulfilled in your hearing" (Luke 4:21). In Him the release Jubilee pictured arrives: freedom from sin's debt.

theology.title: A God who resets
theology.body: Jubilee guaranteed that no family's poverty would become permanent and no family's wealth would grow without limit. The LORD cares about economic structures, not only individual charity. He builds second chances into the system.

application.title: Owner or tenant?
application.body: Israel's land was God's, and they were residents on it. Thinking like a tenant changes how we treat what we hold.
application.question: How would your spending change if you truly believed your money and house belong to God?

application.title: Close enough to redeem
application.body: The kinsman redeemer acted because he was family and had the means. God placed him in that position on purpose.
application.question: Whose struggle are you uniquely positioned to help with because of your relationship or resources?

application.title: Let it rest
application.body: The land rested every seventh year, trusting God to provide (vv. 20–22). Rest required faith that God's provision did not depend on constant work.
application.question: What would it take for you to truly rest one day a week without fearing you will fall behind?

context.heading: Not despised
context.body: God promises to set His dwelling among them and says, "My soul will not ga'al ("despise") you" (v. 11). The same verb returns in verse 44: even in exile, He will not despise them so as to destroy them. The chapter's hardest warnings are bracketed by this promise.

context.heading: When God remembers
context.body: "I will zakhar ("remember") My covenant" (v. 42). In Hebrew, remembering is not recalling forgotten information but acting on a commitment. When God remembered Noah (Genesis 8:1) and Israel in Egypt (Exodus 2:24), rescue followed.

context.heading: Sevenfold and rising
context.body: The warnings come in waves, each "sevenfold" or "seven times" (vv. 18, 21, 24, 28). The structure shows a God who gives repeated chances to turn before the final step of exile. Each wave is an invitation as much as a threat.

theology.title: God among His people
theology.body: "I will walk among you and be your God, and you will be My people" (v. 12). Paul quotes this of the church (2 Corinthians 6:16), and Revelation 21:3 echoes it at the end: God's dwelling is with man. The goal of the covenant is His presence.

theology.title: Faithful when Israel is not
theology.body: Israel did break the covenant and went into exile. But God's covenant with Abraham, Isaac and Jacob held. His faithfulness does not depend on ours, though our response still matters deeply.

application.title: Discipline as invitation
application.body: The rising warnings were meant to bring Israel back before it was too late. Painful consequences can be God's mercy calling us home.
application.question: What painful consequence in your life might be an invitation to turn rather than a punishment to resent?

application.title: Confession that names it
application.body: Verse 40 calls for confessing "their iniquity and that of their fathers." Israel had to own both personal sin and inherited patterns.
application.question: Which pattern from your family's past do you need to honestly name before God?

application.title: Walk with your head up
application.body: God broke Israel's yoke so they could walk upright (v. 13). Shame keeps many believers looking at the ground.
application.question: What shame are you still carrying that God has already broken?

context.heading: Devoted for good
context.body: Anything placed under cherem ("devoted to the LORD") could not be sold or bought back (v. 28). It belonged to God irrevocably. The same word describes things devoted to destruction in the conquest (Joshua 6:17), but here it refers to property given wholly to God's use.

context.heading: The tithe is holy
context.body: "Any ma'aser ("tithe") from the land ... belongs to the LORD; it is holy" (v. 30). The tenth was not a gift Israel chose but a portion God claimed. Christians differ on whether the tithe still binds believers; the New Testament stresses generous, cheerful giving (2 Corinthians 9:7).

context.heading: A price the poor could pay
context.body: If someone vowed but was too poor to pay the standard value, the priest set a price "according to what the one making the vow can afford" (v. 8). God did not want vows to become traps that ruined families.

theology.title: God takes promises seriously
theology.body: Leviticus ends with vows because God expects His people to mean what they say. Ecclesiastes 5:4–5 warns that it is better not to vow than to vow and not pay. God Himself is the great promise keeper.

theology.title: Dedication misused
theology.body: Jesus rebuked people who declared their money "Corban," devoted to God, to avoid supporting their parents (Mark 7:11–13). Even good laws about dedication could be twisted into excuses. God looks at the heart behind the gift.

application.title: Careless promises
application.body: Israelites made vows in crisis and then had to pay when life calmed down. Many of our promises are made in emotion and forgotten in comfort.
application.question: What promise have you made to God or someone else that you have quietly let slide?

application.title: Giving that costs
application.body: The book of holiness ends with money: valuations, redemptions and tithes. Faith that never touches finances is incomplete.
application.question: What does your giving over the last three months say about what you consider holy?

application.title: Gratitude, not bargaining
application.body: Vows were often made in crisis: "If You rescue me, I will give." The law made sure such vows were kept, but the healthiest giving springs from thanks, not deals.
application.question: Are you treating God as a partner to bargain with or a Father to thank?
